title: Russian Refining Watch
dek: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refining: strikes, offline capacity, and the diesel crisis.

claims.text: Russia's Transport Ministry said naval drones struck the Liberian-flagged crude tanker Aframax Rio off the resort city of Sochi on Oct 6, with crude burning openly on the Black Sea; all 23 crew, all Indian nationals, were rescued with no reported injuries. Kyiv had listed the vessel as part of Russia's shadow fleet used to move Russian oil under Western sanctions.

Overnight strikes on Oct 3-4 hit the Lazarevo pumping station on the Surgut-Gorky-Polotsk crude pipeline in the Kirov region, sparked a large fire at the Saratov refinery on the Volga, and set a fuel depot ablaze in Matveyev Kurgan; Moscow-appointed authorities in Crimea restricted gasoline sales without stating a reason.

The Black Sea export port of Novorossiysk suspended oil exports for several days after a major Ukrainian attack on the port early on Oct 2, the same Reuters-sourced reporting said, as Ukraine's campaign widened from refineries to export terminals.

Two merchant vessels were hit by air and sea drones around 3 a.m. on Oct 6 inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, about 112 km off Byala; the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sank with its crew missing and the Palau-flagged Able caught fire, with 18 crew rescued and two injured. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev confirmed the attack, the first on shipping in Bulgarian waters, and called it a gross violation of international law; no party has claimed responsibility.

Bloomberg tanker-tracking data cited by OilPrice.com show Russia's seaborne crude exports averaged 3.62 million barrels per day in the four weeks to September 28, the highest since May 2024, a sign that neither India nor other major buyers have reduced purchases despite US pressure. Russia's oil and gas revenues were nevertheless expected to plunge 23 percent year on year in September on lower crude prices and a stronger ruble, per Reuters calculations cited in the piece.
claims.vintage: Data: four weeks ending Sep 28, 2026; accessed 2026-09-24

claims.text: The Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, the main western outlet for displaced crude, is itself constrained: trader data show exports and transit volumes more than halved from July to August, from 800,000 barrels per day to less than 355,000, after repeated drone strikes collapsed loadings and thinned tanker availability. Chartering a Suezmax tanker to India from Novorossiysk cost about $20 million by the end of August, versus about $13 million a month earlier.

US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff urged Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct 21 to consider resuming US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and to review new ideas on ending the war, Reuters reported. The talks in St. Petersburg, the ninth time Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with Russia releasing Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia. Putin also offered to help US President Donald Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme, and said Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the United States.

Ukraine is launching larger and deeper drone assaults on Russian refineries, storage sites and export facilities after ending its brief adherence to the energy ceasefire that President Donald Trump declared on Oct 11, CNBC reported via TradersUnion on Oct 21. State media reports say more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone, and one of the strikes set an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg on fire. Kpler data show Russia's diesel exports fell more than 75 percent to 141,000 b/d in September from 608,000 b/d in the same period last year, and total diesel exports were around 345,000 b/d so far this year, down 41 percent. Tatiana Mitrova at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy said the scale, range and effectiveness of the strikes have crippled Russian diesel exports, while Kpler's Matt Smith said Trump's arrangement with Putin to increase shipments is likely no longer workable without an energy ceasefire.

Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their main previous customers following the US-brokered lifting of Moscow's export ban, with at least two tankers signalling voyages to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. The tanker Leruo is signalling Manaus, Brazil, after departing the Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct 16, following the tanker Dolunay, which left Primorsk with a diesel cargo on Oct 14 bound for Alanya, Turkey. Turkey has received about 34 percent of Russian diesel loadings so far this year at 95,000 b/d and Brazil about 24 percent at 66,000 b/d, Kpler data show. Russia partially lifted the diesel export ban starting Oct 10; it had reduced exports over the summer before imposing the ban as it grappled with widespread Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries.

Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 b/d in September to 8.43 million b/d, but remained about 870,000 b/d below a year ago, Reuters reported on Oct 20, citing the International Energy Agency's assessment published last week. The year-on-year shortfall sits alongside the refinery outage campaign and the diesel export disruption tracked on this page.

Oil prices fell on Oct 19 as traders weighed possibly higher Russian supplies after US sanctions relief on Friday, Reuters reported, with Brent crude futures down $2.29, or 2.08 percent, to $107.57 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate down $1.95, or 1.92 percent, to $99.46, both pulling back from five-month highs settled on Friday. The waiver follows the deal Trump struck with President Putin for Russia to export diesel to the United States and other countries, starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month before rising to about 7.6 million barrels monthly, Reuters said, adding that Zelenskiy said the US actions will hurt Ukraine and that analysts said mixed messaging on the waiver's details and duration has created uncertainty, so the market is unlikely to fully price in a sustained increase in supply.

President Trump's waiver of Russian sanctions eases energy concerns for India, one of the top importers of Russian oil, and may improve the chances of New Delhi and Washington agreeing on a trade deal, Reuters reported on Oct 19. The Graham Act legislation would have exposed Indian goods to tariffs of up to 100 percent, as India is one of the five largest importers of Russian oil. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrives in India on Tuesday, said trade talks with New Delhi were a consideration for Trump's waiver decision and that the two sides are very close to finalising a trade deal. Earlier this year Russia accounted for nearly half of India's oil imports, but purchases fell in August and continue to decline, Reuters said.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 18 that Russia had deliberately launched at least 76 attacks on energy or oil and gas targets over the past week, including overnight strikes on substations in four regions, and that tens of thousands of families remained without power. Over the week Russia attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, Zelenskiy said.

President Trump said on Oct 17 that he had not announced a final decision on the Russia sanctions he waived a day earlier, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president will take up to 60 days to weigh the economic impact before deciding what comes next, Reuters reported. The Oct 16 executive order used the Graham Act's waiver power to set aside most of the law's new sanctions and its duties, a 500 percent duty on Russian goods and 100 percent duties on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, which were due to take effect Oct 18; sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain in place, and Zelenskyy condemned the waiver.

Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said on Oct 16 that the US Treasury has asked Russia's sovereign wealth fund, the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, to facilitate payments relating to the Trump-Putin deal on the sale of Russian diesel. Dmitriev told an energy conference the Treasury had requested RDIF to facilitate payments and solve tactical issues, and said RDIF will work to ensure that all payments are efficient and reach their intended recipients.

Russia publicly acknowledged the Oct 15 Ukrainian drone strike on the Ryazan refinery on Oct 16 and state TV channel Rossiya-24 broadcast images of the aftermath, the first time state television has shown a refinery attack since the war began, Reuters reported. Moscow is highlighting an attack President Trump has called a disgrace, four days after he announced an energy ceasefire that neither side confirmed; Ukraine said it paused strikes for three days and resumed because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14.

Attacks on Russian refineries have cut an estimated one million tonnes a month of fuel oil supply, Vitol's Asia head Kieran Gallagher said at the SIBCON conference this week, while high-sulphur fuel oil flows through Hormuz, including Iranian supplies, remain down by at least 800,000 tonnes a month from February. Spot premiums for 380-cst high-sulphur fuel oil held near $50 a tonne this week, versus a $5.10 premium on Feb 27, on LSEG data.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian refineries on Oct 15 after a three-day pause, President Zelenskiy told the Financial Times, saying the block on energy strikes was over because Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leaving 600,000 people without power on Oct 14. The Ryazan hit was the first Ukrainian attack on a Russian energy facility since President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Oct 11, a truce neither side confirmed; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no specific agreements had been established.

The IEA said on Oct 14 that a lack of operational Russian refinery capacity meant the recently announced easing of Russian diesel export restrictions was unlikely to bring any material change to the global gasoil balance, and that constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year. The agency put Russian crude production in September at 8.43 million b/d, up 65,000 b/d on the month but 870,000 b/d below a year earlier.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 13 that Ukraine had carried out no strikes on Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since the Oct 11 US announcement of an energy ceasefire, while accusing Russia of continuing to hit Ukrainian energy facilities over the same period.

President Zelenskiy said on Oct 12 that Russia had hit at least six Ukrainian energy targets in overnight strikes despite the energy ceasefire announced by President Trump, and that Moscow had shown no interest in accepting it. The Kremlin was reported as saying it does not want a ceasefire. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Moscow's point man for oil, said Russia would be able to return diesel exports to levels above those outlined in the Trump diesel deal.

On Oct 11 Trump posted that an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine was effective immediately, with neither government confirming any deal. Zelensky said Ukraine would honor it if Russia reciprocated, but Russian strikes on Ukrainian power facilities continued afterward and the Kremlin made no public commitment.

Axios, citing a US official, reported Trump moved ahead with the Russian diesel waiver after Zelensky ignored about six US requests to stop hitting Russian refineries; during Oct 9 talks in Miami, envoys Witkoff and Kushner told Ukraine's delegation the waiver was coming because the strikes were 'directly affecting U.S. consumers'.

President Trump said after a phone call with Vladimir Putin that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons 'immediately thereafter,' and 3 million more 'within a short period.' Treasury immediately issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, the first diesel easing longer than the standard 30-day window; Deputy PM Novak told Tass Russia is lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with US-bound supplies possible in October. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the strikes.

Russia's State Duma budget and tax committee backed draft Tax Code amendments extending an existing fuel-import subsidy to large-scale seaborne gasoline imports from India, with the subsidy calculated off an indicative Indian gasoline price plus shipping costs. Operating refineries are producing about 85,000 tonnes of gasoline per day against demand of around 111,000 tonnes, leaving a structural shortfall near 25,000 tonnes a day, roughly 20% of consumption.
claims.source: Investment Guru India (via Kyiv Post, citing RBC)

claims.text: In a rare acknowledgment at the Oct 1 Valdai Club session, Putin said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries had cost Russia roughly 1% of GDP and conceded Kyiv had partially achieved its goal of damaging the economy, while offering no ceasefire and saying Russia would prefer talks.

Drones launched a massive attack on the Moscow region overnight on Oct 22, with the 75 Arsenal military plant in Serpukhov among the targets, EuropeSays reported citing The Moscow Times via Ukrinform. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 630 drones had been heading toward Moscow since the evening of Oct 21, 163 of which were shot down during the attack on the city, and two people were injured in the area of the village of Voronovo. According to Astra, drones attacked the 75 Arsenal plant and footage recorded by eyewitnesses showed an explosion and fire at the facility following the drone strikes. No refinery hit was confirmed in this report.
claims.source: EuropeSays (citing The Moscow Times via Ukrinform)

claims.text: Satellite imagery published on Oct 20 indicates that Ukraine's Oct 10 strike against the NZNP oil-loading terminal in Rostov Oblast damaged eight oil storage tanks, each with a capacity of 5,000 cubic metres, the Institute for the Study of War assessment for Oct 21 reported via EuropeSays. The terminal loads petroleum products from the Novoshakhtinsk refinery onto river-sea tankers for export.
claims.source: EuropeSays (citing Institute for the Study of War)

claims.text: A fire broke out at an oil pumping station near Michurinsk in Russia's Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels reported by the Kyiv Independent via EuropeSays. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire on the territory of one of the enterprises in Michurinsky District without naming the facility, claimed four drones were shot down, and reported no casualties. Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near Novonikolskoye, a Transneft facility on the Druzhba pipeline network about 350 to 400 kilometres from the front line, which Ukraine previously attacked on Aug 18, 2025, when the strike halted Druzhba operation. Ukrainian authorities did not confirm the attack and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.

Reports on Oct 20 confirmed the damage from the Oct 17-18 Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg, Tank Storage Magazine reported: at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, three storage tanks caught fire, with two damaged and one completely destroyed; at the Ruchyi oil depot, one vertical steel tank was destroyed and another damaged. A large scale fire at the Ozon logistics hub affected more than 10,000 square metres, and the Southern Fairway Bridge and the Finland Railway Bridge were both damaged. One person was confirmed killed and 15 others injured in the overall attack, which involved over 1,000 drones launched at the terminal, the depot, the logistics hub and the bridges.

The St. Petersburg oil terminal struck on Oct 18 exports about 120,000 b/d of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler cited by CNBC on Oct 19, and it is unclear how bad the damage at the facility is. Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after President Trump declared on Oct 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce, but Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after that announcement and President Zelenskiy said last week Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian facilities in retaliation.

Ukraine launched one of the largest drone attacks of the war overnight Oct 17-18, striking the St. Petersburg oil terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, with fires also reported at industrial warehouses in the city's Kolpinsky District, St. Petersburg governor Alexander Beglov said. One person was killed and five injured in St. Petersburg, and two transformer substations struck at Yanino in the Leningrad region left about 20,000 people without electricity on Sunday morning. Russia's Defence Ministry said air defences shot down some 1,015 drones near Moscow and several other western regions.

Reuters reported on Oct 16, citing unnamed industry sources, that Rosneft's Ryazan refinery suspended operations at one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, following the drone attack on Oct 15. The same unit had already been shut after a drone strike in September. The refinery's three other primary crude distillation units, CDU-1, CDU-3 and CDU-4, reportedly continue to operate.

A large Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire at Rosneft's Ryazan refinery early on Oct 15, regional governor Pavel Malkov said, with damage still being assessed and emergency services at the scene. The plant, about 300 km southeast of Moscow, supplies fuel to the capital and accounts for almost 5 percent of Russian refining throughput; it has been hit several times in recent months.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence said its forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, per ArmyInform reporting on Oct 12, with Lukoil's Perm refinery, about 1,500 km from the border, the farthest on the list. Monitoring by Euromaidan Press found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the sources it tracks since the Oct 11 ceasefire announcement.

Ukraine's military confirmed long-range drones struck Tatneft's TANECO refinery at Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan on Oct 12, about 750 miles from the Ukrainian border, as part of a wider attack on industrial targets in the region. Tatarstan's leader said the attack killed at least 13 people, including a child, and wounded 39. TANECO processed 17 million tons of crude in 2024, producing 2.7 million tons of gasoline and 8.5 million tons of diesel, and had been hit before in early June.

Three of Russia's six largest diesel-producing refineries are now shut or running at roughly one-quarter capacity, according to Reuters calculations cited Oct 12: Kirishi is completely offline, Volgograd and NORSI are at about 25 percent of nameplate, and TANECO was struck on Sunday Oct 11. The six plants, Omsk, Kirishi, TANECO, Volgograd, NORSI and Perm, together account for roughly half of Russian diesel production.

Ukraine struck the Samara linear production and dispatch station, a Transneft Urals-blend hub, for the third time this month overnight Oct 9-10; the Ukrainian General Staff said the earlier Oct 2 and Oct 7 hits caused extensive damage to storage tanks and associated infrastructure at the junction.

Ukrainian drones struck the Novoshakhtinsk/Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don overnight Oct 9-10, starting a major fire at the export-loading facility; the regional governor confirmed two ships damaged at the Port of Azov and a rail bridge strike in the same wave.

Ukraine attacked Lukoil's Ukhta oil-processing plant in the Komi Republic, the fourth Russian refinery hit this week after Omsk, Salavat and the Astrakhan gas plant, President Zelenskyy confirmed Friday; the plant's design capacity is about 80,000 b/d, and Bloomberg calculates the four facilities hit this week total about 720,000 b/d of crude capacity plus up to 12 Bcm per year of gas.

Ukraine's General Staff said it struck Russia's largest refinery, the Gazprom Neft Omsk plant (about 440,000 b/d, roughly one-fifteenth of national capacity), overnight Oct 8, some 2,500-2,700 km from Ukraine; regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed a drone hit an industrial zone. It is the second strike on Omsk since July 6, and Zelenskyy called it an 'important achievement,' saying 'Siberia, too, is now within reach.'

In the same overnight wave, Ukraine's military said it struck the Ust-Luga and Vysotsk ports, which handle Baltic Sea oil exports, plus targets in the Kaluga and Yaroslavl regions, with local governors confirming the attacks; the strikes widen the campaign from refineries to export infrastructure.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct 8 that the Oct 2 strike on the Samara linear production and dispatch station at Prosvet damaged 11 RVS-20000 tanks, 3 RVS-50000 tanks, pipeline sections and an automated oil loading station; the hub blends Urals export crude and, per the General Staff, handles up to half of Russia's oil exports.

Ukraine's General Staff claimed an overnight strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery complex in Bashkortostan, described as one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities, about 750 miles east of Moscow; local authorities had not confirmed the claim. The 200 kb/d plant was previously hit on July 14 and September 24, when its AVT-6 primary unit caught fire.

President Zelenskyy said on Oct 7 that Ukrainian forces struck two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions over the past day, calling them 'justified responses' to Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Rosneft's Ryazan refinery, Russia's fourth-largest at more than 260,000 b/d, suspended crude processing after a weekend drone attack; Reuters industry sources said the plant is expected to stay idle until the end of the month with no product loadings planned before Dec 1, and a second crude unit is under repair after an earlier strike that took about 80,000 b/d offline.

Overnight on Oct 5-6, Ukraine launched what Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin called one of the largest drone attacks on the capital region in two years, with about 650 drones approaching and 105 downed near the city; the regional governor reported one fatality and six injured. Monitoring channels and eyewitness footage showed flames and heavy smoke at the Volodarskaya linear production and dispatch station near Konstantinovo, Transneft's largest Moscow-region oil depot at about 3 million tons a year, which supplies fuel to the capital's three main airports; Russian authorities have not confirmed damage at the depot itself.
claims.source: The Gaze (citing Astra and eyewitness footage)

claims.text: Ukraine's General Staff said a drone strike ignited fires at the port of Taman in the Krasnodar region, damaging an oil storage tank, a warehouse and terminals, with regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev reporting two people wounded. The same statement said a Pantsir-S1 air defense system in occupied Crimea was also hit.

Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the October 1-2 strikes on the Lukoil-Volgogradneftepererabotka refinery, one of Russia's largest at about 15 million tons per year, and on Transneft's Samara tank farm plus the Samara-1 and Samara-2 pumping stations; analysts described the Samara facility as Europe's largest tank farm. Russia's defense ministry claimed to have intercepted 646 drones in the same overnight wave.

Coordinated Ukrainian strikes overnight hit the LUKOIL-Volgograd refinery and the Samara oil dispatch station near Prosvet, Ukrainian authorities said. Explosions and fires were recorded at both sites; NASA's FIRMS satellite service registered fire hotspots at key processing units of the Volgograd refinery, which handles about 15 million tons of crude a year and has been repeatedly targeted. The Samara station blends different crude grades into Russia's main Urals export stream and was previously struck in April, when five crude tanks were damaged.
Russia's second-largest refinery, Kirishi, halted processing on September 29 after Ukrainian drone attacks damaged three of its four crude distillation units, two industry sources told Reuters.

Russia raised its expected idle primary refining capacity for October by 67% versus the earlier plan to 4.0 million tons, per Reuters industry-source estimates, after postponed maintenance at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery and a unit of Lukoil's NORSI; Rosneft's Tuapse refinery also reportedly halted crude processing on Oct 1 on low margins. More than half of October's idle capacity is expected to return in November, with November idle at 1.2 to 1.8 million tons.

The Associated Press reported on Oct 4 that the International Energy Agency estimates a Russian refinery has been successfully struck by a drone roughly once every three days in recent months. The cadence is consistent with a sustained attrition campaign but is not an independent confirmation of Ukraine's claim, which AP noted it could not verify, that 51% of Russian refining capacity is out of action.

Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on October 4 that long-range strikes have put 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity out of action, citing strikes on refineries in Moscow, Yaroslavl, Perm, Saratov and Syzran plus the Kirishi (Kinef) and Ust-Luga plants. The claim could not be independently verified. President Vladimir Putin told the Valdai forum on October 1 that the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of gross domestic product (GDP), while International Energy Agency (IEA) data cited in the report says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30%, with drivers queuing up to 40 hours at filling stations and Moscow banning diesel exports.

Ukraine's Defense Intelligence representative Andrii Yusov said Ukrainian forces have conducted 64 targeted strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure facilities this year, destroying or damaging about one-third of the targeted refineries and storage facilities, and said the strikes compound Western sanctions that restrict imports of repair equipment. The agency framed the disruption as long-term pressure on Russian military logistics. This is a Ukrainian claim, not independently verified.
